manuscript.title: A cost-efficient IoT service placement approach using whale optimization algorithm in fog computing environment
manuscript.abstract_text: The rapid development of Internet of Things (IoT)-based applications and the era of 5G networks has led to an exponential increase in the amount of data required for processing the IoT services. The fog computing paradigm has emerged as a distributed computing solution for serving these applications using available fog nodes near the IoT devices. Since the IoT applications are developed in the form of several IoT services with various quality of service (QoS) requirements that can be deployed on the fog nodes with different resource capabilities in the fog ecosystem, finding an efficient service placement plan is one of the challenging issues to be considered. In this paper, we propose an efficient IoT service placement solution based on the autonomic methodology for deploying IoT applications on the fog infrastructure. Our proposed solution monitors the QoS requirements of IoT services and capabilities of available fog nodes to determine an efficient service placement plan using the whale opti­ mization algorithm (WOA) meta-heuristic technique. Besides, our evolutionary-based mechanism utilized the throughput and the energy consumption as objective functions for finding desirable IoT service placement plan while meeting the QoS requirements of each IoT service. Also, we develop an autonomous service placement framework according to a three-tier architecture of the fog ecosystem to show the interaction between the main components of the IoT device and fog layers for deploying IoT applications. The simulation results demonstrate that the proposed solution increases the resource usage and service acceptance ratio and reduces the service delay and the energy consumption compared with the other metaheuristic-based mechanisms.

sections.body_text:
In recent years, the fog computing paradigm emerged as a distrib­
uted computing paradigm to provide storage, computing, and
networking capabilities for serving the Internet of Things (IoT) appli­
cations at the edge of the network (Atlam, Walters, & Wills, 2018, Brogi,
Forti, Guerrero, & Lera, 2019). Fog computing technology deploys IoT
applications on the available fog resources to minimize cost, latency,
bandwidth usage, and satisfy the quality of service (QoS) requirements
for real-time applications such as virtual reality, autonomous cars,
augmented reality, real-time manufacturing, drones, and cyber-physical
system in IoT networks (Yousefpour et al., 2019). According to micro-
service architecture, the IoT applications are developed in the form of
several IoT services that are loosely coupled with various QoS re­
quirements that can deploy in different locations. On the other hand, in
the fog ecosystem, the fog layer consists of a network of resource-limited
fog nodes with different resource capabilities. The IoT service placement
problem is deploying IoT services on the fog nodes with different
resource capabilities while satisfying various QoS requirements of IoT
services (Omer Hassan, Azizi, & Shojafar, 2020). It has a considerable
impact on the performance and energy consumption of fog resources in
the fog ecosystem. Some IoT applications are delay-sensitive, such as
virtual reality and online gaming, while others are compute-intensive,
such as big data analytics applications. On the other hand, due to the
heterogeneity and resource-limited fog nodes and various requirements
of IoT applications, providing an effective placement plan is one of the
most challenging tasks that should be considered. Evolutionary algo­
rithms are a subset of optimization techniques inspired by natural evo­
lution operators such as mutation, selection, and crossover within
specific constraints to solve service placement problems. Since the ser­
vice placement problem is known as an NP-hard optimization problem,
the evolutionary algorithms such as genetic algorithm (GA) (Skarlat,
Nardelli, Schulte, Borkowski, & Leitner, 2017, Guerrero, Lera, & Juiz,
2019a, Canali & Lancellotti, 2019), particle swarm optimization (PSO)
(Djemai, Stolf, Monteil, & Pierson, 2019, Roy et al., 2020), and Simu­
lated Annealing (SA) (Santoyo-Gonz´alez & Cervell´o-Pastor, 2018) are

utilized to calculate near-optimal solutions in an enormous solution
space. Therefore, the service placement problem as one of the main open
issues can play an effective role in resource management scope, and it
has a significant impact on the bandwidth usage and latency of IoT
networks. Although some service placement mechanisms have already
been investigated to find the sub-optimal service placement solutions,
still more work is required for deploying IoT services better
automatically.
In this study, we present an efficient IoT service placement solution
inspired by using the autonomic computing paradigm for deploying IoT
applications on the virtualized fog infrastructure. Our solution conforms
to a model presented by IBM (Huebscher & McCann, 2008), which in­
cludes four phases: monitoring, analysis, planning, and execution with a
shared knowledge base named MAPE-k loop for placing IoT services on
the fog nodes according to their QoS requirements, automatically. First,
the needed information about the QoS requirements of IoT services and
capabilities of available fog nodes is continuously gathered in the
monitoring phase. The collected information is used to prioritize IoT
services based on their deadline and waiting time. Then, in the planning
phase, an appropriate placement solution using the whale optimization
algorithm (WOA) meta-heuristic technique (Mirjalili, Mirjalili, & Lewis,
2014a, Gharehchopogh & Gholizadeh, 2019) is determined. The WOA as
an evolutionary algorithm is suitable for solving optimization problems
according to exploration and exploitation phases to find cost-efficient
solutions into search space. The WOA as a population-based meta-heu­
ristic technique utilises the exploration and exploitation phases in each
iteration. It provides high convergence speed and local optima avoid­
ance during the search process compared with existing evolutionary
algorithms (e.g., GA, SA, PSO, etc.). Besides, the WOA technique has
been successfully utilized to solve engineering optimization problems in
various scopes including cloud computing (Abdel-Basset, Abdle-Fatah,
& Sangaiah, 2019a, Revathi, Ramaraj, & Chithra, 2019), image pro­
cessing (Abdel-Basset, Chang, & Mohamed, 2020b, Mostafa, Hassanien,
Houseni, & Hefny, 2017), social network (Jain, Katarya, & Sachdeva,
2020, Ala’M, Faris, Alqatawna, & Hassonah, 2018), data mining
(Mafarja & Mirjalili, 2017, Chen et al., 2019), and IoT (Maddikunta
et al., 2020, Reddy & Babu, 2019). Finally, the achieved placement
solution using the WOA technique is executed in the execution phase.
These four phases are continuously performed at pre-specified time in­
tervals and deploy the IoT services on the available fog nodes corre­
sponding to their QoS requirements.
The main contributions of this work can be summarized as follows:
• Designing an autonomous service placement framework according to
the three-tier architecture of the fog ecosystem to show the inter­
action between main components into IoT devices and fog layers.
• Proposing an efficient service placement algorithm using WOA meta-
heuristic technique for deploying IoT applications on the virtualized
fog infrastructure.
• Validating the proposed solution through a series of experiments in
terms of resource usage, service acceptance ratio, service delay, and
energy consumption metrics.
The rest of this study is organized as follows: In Section 2, we review
the related researches about service placement in fog computing. Sec­
tion 3 provides the preliminary concepts for the proposal of this work. In
Section 4, we explain the proposed solution in more detail. In Section 5,
we discuss the obtained simulation results, and we finally present the
conclusions and future works in Section 6.
2.

In this section, we will review the application placement mechanisms
in the fog/edge computing environment. Then, we summarize different
works to solve the application placement problem.
Skarlat et al. (Skarlat et al., 2017) have presented a service
placement solution using a genetic algorithm in a fog computing
network. Their solution considers the application QoS requirements and
the fog resources heterogeneity to achieve a suitable placement plan.
Besides, they described a conceptual hierarchical framework by intro­
ducing fog orchestration nodes to manage several fog colonies. Their
obtained results demonstrated that their proposed solution improves in
terms of fog resources utilization and IoT service execution time
compared with other approaches. Guerrero et al. (Guerrero et al., 2019)
have studied the suitability of various metaheuristic-based techniques
for the IoT service placemen in the fog computing environment. Their
study adapted three evolutionary algorithms to the specific scope by
defining a set of evolutionary operators and optimizing evolutionary
algorithms. Besides, they formalized three objective functions: minimi­
zation of latency, resource usage, and service spread. Their results
illustrated that the NSGA-II algorithm is superior to other evolutionary
algorithms in terms of mentioned objective functions. Canali et al.
(Canali & Lancellotti, 2019) have proposed an optimization solution for
allocating data sensor workload on fog devices. Their solution considers
the processing time and communication latency between IoT devices
and fog devices. Also, they presented a heuristic-based mechanism using
a genetic algorithm to achieve a scalable solution for large-scale service
placement issues. They evaluated their solution on the smart city
application and demonstrated that they achieve the best solution than
other evolutionary algorithms. Djemai et al. (Djemai et al., 2019) have
proposed an IoT service placement approach using discrete particle
swarm optimization, which considers service delay for minimizing en­
ergy consumption. Their approach considers various logical topologies
for IoT applications with service delay requirements to achieve a delay-
energy trade-off. According to their simulation results, their proposed
approach prefers the fog layer, then depending on the IoT application, it
selects between the IoT device and cloud layer.
Roy et al. (Roy et al., 2020) have studied the multimedia service
placement problem in the mobile edge computing network. They
formulated their problem as a linear programming formulation and
utilized particle swarm optimization as a meta-heuristic mechanism to
solve their problem within polynomial time. Gonz´alez et al. (Santoyo-
Gonz´alez & Cervell´o-Pastor, 2018) have proposed a latency-aware
strategy for fog service placement under 5G mobile network. They
mathematically formulated the fog service placement problem in the
form of a mixed-integer linear programming model. They presented a
hybrid heuristic-based mechanism using simulated annealing according
to the traffic generator’s place to solve the formulated problem. Finally,
they developed a desktop application to obtain the flexibility and us­
ability of the proposed strategy. In (Guerrero, Lera, & Juiz, 2019b), a
decentralized mechanism has been proposed to solve service placement
problems in a fog computing environment. Their mechanism considers
usage data and performance obtained in each fog node, and it is locally
performed in each fog node to migrate micro-services to upper fog
nodes. Besides, their mechanism considers the interoperability and
migration between the micro-services. They validated their mechanism
using the iFogSim toolkit by modelling microservice-based applications
and indicated that their solution improves service latency and network
usage compared with other mechanisms. Lin et al. (Lin, Deng,
Suwatcharachaitiwong, & Li, 2020) have proposed a bat-inspired algo­
rithm to solve IoT service placement in the fog landscape. Their pro­
posed solution simulates the food-searching behaviour of bats for
deploying weighted fog devices to achieve a better solution than the
PSO-based approach. Forti et al. (Forti, Ferrari, & Brogi, 2020) have
developed a methodology using declarative programming called SecFog
for mapping IoT services with various security requirements on fog
devices with different security capabilities. Their methodology con­
siders the trust model among various stakeholders by managing fog
infrastructures to determine the most secure service deployments using
reducing manual tuning. They prototyped their methodology using
ProbLog language for deploying IoT services to achieve appropriate
trade-offs between the required security level and energy consumption.

Mehran et al. (Mehran, Kimovski, & Prodan, 2019) have proposed a
multi-objective approach using the Pareto-based search technique for
placing IoT applications by considering computation and communica­
tion perspectives in a fog environment. Their approach utilized a finite
state machine to model IoT applications. It used a genetic multi-
objective optimization technique to find a trade-off between three ob­
jectives, namely energy consumption, completion time, and total cost.
They evaluated their proposed approach on simulated and real-world
fog infrastructure testbed for various medical IoT applications. They
demonstrated that their approach reduces completion time and energy
consumption compared with existing approaches.
In (Mahmud, Ramamohanarao, & Buyya, 2018), a latency-aware
application placement mechanism for deploying IoT applications on
fog devices to satisfy their QoS requirements has been proposed. Their
mechanism aims to address both deadlines based QoS of IoT applications
along with optimizing resources in the fog ecosystem. The proposed
mechanism consists of two heuristics: the first heuristic is about IoT
service placement and the second heuristic is about dispatching IoT
service towards the inactive fog resources. Lera et al. (Lera, Guerrero, &
Juiz, 2019) have used a multi-criteria decision analysis technique for the
fog service placement problem. Their approach utilized a decision model
to determine the most suitable placement plan by ranking alternatives.
Besides, they used the hop count, latency, energy consumption, and cost
metrics for ranking placement alternatives. They compared their
approach with the weighted average technique under various weights of
each metric to make the mapping of IoT applications more efficient. Shih
et al. (Shih, Wang, & Pang, 2019) have designed a game theory-based
approach for fog computing service deployment problems. Their
approach utilized the Nash bargaining technique for modelling inter­
action among the network operators and the various application pro­
viders in the form of the one-to-many bargaining game. Besides, they
proposed a queuing model for predicting the required fog resource to
meet delay requirements of concurrent applications. Yadav et al. (Yadav
et al., 2019) have proposed a hybrid approach using particle swarm
optimization and genetic algorithm to place IoT services on the fog
infrastructure. Their proposed approach efficiently allocates the IoT
services for minimizing makespan and energy consumption. Their ob­
tained results illustrated that the hybrid proposed approach is superior
to particle swarm optimization and genetic algorithm methods for ser­
vice allocation, individually. Zeng et al. (Zeng, Gu, & Yao, 2018) have
developed an energy-aware service placement approach for cyber-
physical system applications in the fog computing environment. They
formulated the energy efficiency service problem in the form of mixed-
integer linear programming. According to the presented formulation,
they proposed a low-complexity heuristic using a relaxation strategy to
deal with computation complexity. Their results demonstrated the high
energy efficiency of the proposed approach compared with existing
methods. Lee et al. (Lee, Chung, & Kim, 2019) have presented a practical
fog server deployment mechanism for minimizing the data movement
using the vector bin packing technique in a fog network. Their proposed
mechanism considers the different issues, and it uses the computing
resource of fog devices as efficiently as for processing more IoT services.
Besides, it replaces the fog device periodically corresponding with the
changing IoT service environment to provide quick service execution
time in a dynamic environment. Their experimental results showed that
their proposed mechanism could reduce the data movement and in­
crease the resource utilization of fog devices.
Cheng et al. (Cheng et al., 2017) have introduced a situation-aware
IoT applications coordination mechanism. They considered formal sit­
uation patterns and provided an automaton-aware situational event
detection mechanism. Besides, they proposed situational event-based
service coordination to generate an execution sequence for IoT ser­
vices. Zhou et al. (Zhou, Liao, Zhao, Ai, & Guizani, 2019) have designed
a contract-based server recruitment method for sharing resources in the
vehicular fog computing ecosystem. Besides, they proposed a matching-
based reliable task offloading under incomplete information for
minimizing the delay network. Their results indicated that their pro­
posed solution could efficiently simulate resource sharing and discover
the optimal solution in a polynomial time.
Liao et al. (Liao et al., 2020) have proposed a blockchain-enabled
task offloading strategy to enhance security in the vehicular fog
computing ecosystem. Their proposed strategy guarantees fairness, se­
curity, and privacy while reducing queuing-delay, trustfulness, and
handover-cost. Furthermore, they conducted a security analysis to prove
their proposed strategy’s feasibility, efficiency, and reliability. They
conducted a performance evaluation to illustrate that their solution
enhanced the convergence speed. Shi et al. (Shi, Du, Wang, Wang, &
Yuan, 2020) have studied the task allocation problem in the dynamic
vehicular fog-enabled environment. They formulated their problem in a
Markov decision process to maximise the average latency-aware utility
of offloading tasks in a time interval. Then, they used a deep rein­
forcement learning-based mechanism to enhance the entropy of policy
and the expected reward. Nayeri et al. (Nayeri, Ghafarian, & Javadi,
2021) have investigated and analyzed the application placement
mechanisms using Artificial intelligence (AI) techniques. They catego­
rized the AI-based placement mechanisms into three classes:
evolutionary-based algorithms, machine learning-based algorithms, and
combinatorial-based algorithms. Besides, they discussed IoT application
placemen’s security aspects and provided the open issues as future di­
rections. Sonkoly et al. (Sonkoly, Czentye, Szalay, N´emeth, & Toka,
2021) have provided a comprehensive review and a taxonomy on the
application placement in edge ecosystems. They categorized the service
placement mechanisms in terms of utilized mathematical models,
objective functions, constraints, and time complexity. Then, summarize
the main lessons learned and present some research gaps in the current
research studies.
As mentioned above, most of the research works focus on heuristic-
based or meta-heuristic-based strategies to address the IoT service
placement problem on the fog infrastructure. Since the resource usage
pattern in some IoT applications is dynamic and changes over time, fog
nodes are resource-limited and heterogeneous. Therefore, the heuristic-
based mechanisms may not be appropriate in such situations. Therefore,
providing an effective placement plan can play an effective role in
resource management scope to achieve better performance and quicker
convergence in an autonomic manner. Therefore, we combine the WOA
technique as a metaheuristic-based technique with the MAPE-K control
loop as an autonomic computing model to deploy IoT services on the fog
nodes. Although some mechanisms (Skarlat et al., 2017, Guerrero et al.,
2019a, Canali & Lancellotti, 2019, Djemai et al., 2019, Roy et al., 2020,
Santoyo-Gonz´alez & Cervell´o-Pastor, 2018) have already utilized the
meta heuristic-based techniques for addressing the IoT service place­
ment problem, more work is still required for deploying IoT applications
on the fog infrastructure in an efficient fashion.

nisms, a comparison of them in terms of the evaluation tools and met­
rics, technique used, performance metric, deployment strategy(e.g.,

This section briefly describes the whale optimization algorithm
(WOA) technique and autonomic computing methodology.
3.1.

The WOA is a population-based meta-heuristic technique introduced
by Mirjalili (Mirjalili, Mirjalili, Saremi, & Mirjalili, 2020b), which
models the hunting behaviour of whales as the search agents in the state
space. The humpback whales are certain kinds of whales that use the
bubble-net feeding mechanism by generating bubbles in a spiral path to
hunt their prey. The WOA technique used three evolutionary operators

search in the state space. In the encircling prey phase, the whales, as the
search agents can identify the position of prey and encompass them. The
WOA technique considers the best-obtained solution as target prey, and
other search agents attempt to modify their positions around the optimal
solution. In the exploitation phase, the whales attack towards the prey
using a bubble-net feeding mechanism. To do this, the WOA technique
calculates the distance between the prey position and the whale position
through a spiral model or the shrinking encircling mechanisms to
modify the location of whales during the search process. Finally, in the
exploration phase, the whales seek randomly for achieving the best so­
lution and modify their locations according to the location of other
search agents using a random solution instead of the best solution.
Note that the WOA technique estimates the distance between the
whale (i.e., current solution) placed at position (X, Y) and prey (i.e., best
solution) placed at position (X*, Y*) to calculate the fitness function of
whales, as shown in Fig. 1. To do this, a spiral equation is utilized to

autonomic computing scope, the four main properties including self-
configuration, self-healing, self-protection, and self-optimization are
considered as self-management capabilities for any autonomous system.
The self-configuration property refers to adjusting the initialization
parameters and the deployment conditions to install and configure the
computer systems according to high-level policies, automatically. The
self-healing property refers to diagnosing and recovering unexpected
problems such as hardware and software failures to enhance the avail­
ability and reliability of computer systems. Fault tolerance is considered
as the main aspect of the self-healing feature. The self-protection prop­
erty refers to forecasting, identifying, and preventing various attacks to
protect computer system integrity and privacy. Security is considered as
the main aspect of the self-protection feature. Finally, the self-
optimization property refers to seeking and recognizing opportunities
to improve quality of service (QoS) or system performance according to
predefined goals, proactively (Parashar et al., 2018). To achieve these
self-management capabilities, IBM proposed MAPE-K (Monitoring,
Analyzing, Planning, Execution, Knowledge) loop as a reference logical
architecture to realize autonomous management of computer systems,
as shown in Fig. 3. Firstly, the monitoring step captures the context and
information (e.g., network usage, CPU utilization) through sensors from
a dynamic environment or managed element (e.g., a computer network).
Then, the analyzing step aggregates, filters, and transforms the captured
information to make a comprehensive model to diagnose abnormal sit­
uations, predict situations, and describe more desirable situations. The
planning step includes making a decision plan using event-condition-
action rules to transfer from a current situation to the desired situa­
tion. Finally, the execution step implements the decisions determined by
the planning step in order to react to environmental evolutions through
effectors on the managed element. Besides, the knowledge is a shared
database among the different steps to storage and exchange of events.
4.

In this section, we explain an autonomic-based IoT service placement
approach in more detail. We first develop an autonomous service
placement framework for deploying IoT applications into the three-tier
fog landscape. Then, we provide a formulation for the IoT service
placement problem. Finally, an efficient service placement algorithm
using the WOA technique to deploy the IoT services is described.
4.1.

In this section, an autonomous framework for deploying IoT services
on the virtual fog infrastructure to fulfil the proposed solution will be
described, as shown in Fig. 4. The proposed framework includes three
layers: the thing layer, the fog layer, and the cloud layer. The thing layer
as the bottom layer consists of a series of smart objects such as tablets
and mobile phones to gather the required information from the fog
landscape. The fog layer as the main layer is located between the thing
and cloud layers and includes a set of slave fog domains to handle the
IoT user requests in different geo-distributed locations. Each fog domain
consists of several fog nodes with different resource capabilities to serve
IoT services according to their QoS requirements and a domain control
node. The master fog domain is responsible for determining the strategy
of the dispatch and deployment of the IoT services among the fog do­
mains in certain Δt time intervals according to the autonomic computing
model. It keeps the collected information about fog nodes through the
control nodes of each slave fog domain into the shared knowledge base.

MAPE-k loop to automatically place IoT services on the fog nodes ac­
cording to their QoS requirements.

cooperate in a master/slave manner. The fog domains are micro-data
centres that include a set of fog nodes and a fog domain control node.

The admission control component receives IoT services through the
fog gateway from the thing layer and delivers them to the fog layer or
the cloud layer. According to their deadline parameter, it verifies IoT
services to send the delay-sensitive services to the master fog domain for
deploying on the fog infrastructure and other IoT services through cloud
gateway to the cloud layer are transferred, as shown in Fig. 5. When IoT
services arrive into the master fog domain component, it utilized the
MAPE-k loop to automatically place IoT services on the fog nodes ac­
cording to their QoS requirements.
4.1.3. Slave fog domains
We consider several fog domains in the fog ecosystem which together
cooperate in a master/slave manner. The fog domains are micro-data
centres that include a set of fog nodes and a fog domain control node.
Each fog node as a computational resource provides the processing
power, memory, and storage capabilities for deploying and serving the
IoT services. The fog domain control node is a powerful fog node in

4.1.4.

The master fog domain as the most important component in the fog
landscape is responsible for managing and deploying the IoT services
received from the admission control component in an autonomic
fashion. It keeps the required information about the QoS requirements of
IoT services and capabilities of available fog nodes into its knowledge
base. Therefore, it utilized the MAPE-k loop to dispatch IoT services
between the suitable slave fog domains. The master fog domain acts
according to four sub-components: monitor, analyzer, planner, and
executor. The monitor sub-component gathers the required information
about the capabilities of available fog nodes and QoS requirements of
IoT services and stores them into the shared database to use by others.
The analyzer sub-component prioritizes IoT services using the infor­
mation collected (i.e., deadline and waiting time) by the monitor. Then,
the planner component as the core of the master fog domain determines
an appropriate placement plan using the WOA technique and then saves
it into the knowledge base to be used by the executor sub-component.
Finally, the determined placement solution is performed by the exec­
utor. These sub-components regularly cooperated at given time intervals
to deploy the IoT services on the suitable fog nodes according to their
QoS requirements.

gateway. The cloud servers provide the storage and processing capa­
bilities to serve IoT applications based on the pay-per-use model. The
cloud servers serve compute-intensive or data-intensive IoT applica­
tions, which require heavy compute processing and storage capabilities
in a long time interval. Note that the complementary functions of fog

The time complexity of the proposed algorithm depends on the
required time for generating the initial population, calculating the
fitness function, and the main body of the proposed algorithm including
the exploration and exploration phases. The time complexity of gener­
ating the initial population (lines 2–8) depends on the population size (i.
e., N) and the size of each candidate solution (i.e., J), and it is equal
toO(J × N). The computational complexity of the fitness function (i.
e.,O(fitness)) to calculate the value of candidate solutions and it is
specified by the application which depends on the number of IoT service
and the number of fog nodes. Since solutions are illustrated with a
matrix W of the size |L| × |J| where |L| is the number of IoT services and
|J| is the number of fog nodes. Therefore, the computational complexity
of the fitness function can be specified asO(fitness) = O(L × J). Also, the
time complexity of the main loop (lines 11–28) depends on the
maximum number of iteration, the population size, and the size of each
candidate solution and it is expressed byO(Maxt × N × (J + O(fitness))).
Since N, Maxt and O(fitness) are linear with respect to n, the total time
complexity of the proposed algorithm can be described asO(J × N) +
O(Maxt × N × (J + O(fitness))) ≅O(n3). Therefore, the WOA-FSP algo­
rithm is an approximation solution with polynomial time complexity.

5.1.

In this section, we provide the simulation setting to develop exper­
iments for validating the effectiveness of the proposed approach in more
detail. To model and simulate the fog ecosystem and IoT services, we
utilize the iFogSim toolkit (Gupta, Vahid Dastjerdi, Ghosh, & Buyya,
2017) with some modifications of the classes to characterize the fog
infrastructure, IoT applications, and resource management algorithms.
It provided a series of classes for modelling fog infrastructure (e.g.,
Sensor, Actuator, and Fog.
Device classes) and IoT applications (e.g., AppEdge, AppModule, and
AppLoop classes). In this study, we use three main class categories,
namely: physical, logical, and control to simulate and validate our
proposed service placement solution in the iFogSim library. The physical
entities include IoT sensors, gateways, fog devices, cloud servers, links,
and they have been implemented by the classes of FogDevice, Sensor,
Actuator, and Tuple. The FogDevice class is one of the most important
classes of the iFogSim library to model fog nodes, and it is expressed by
its resource attributes include the power processing, the main memory,
and the disk capacities, and the network bandwidth. The Sensor class is
utilized to model the IoT devices into the IoT layer to generate tuples
according to Table 3. The Actuator class has utilized the tuples of fog
devices to determine and perform the placement plan. The Tuple is a
class to simulate the data flow among the entities according to the
triggered events in the fog environment, and it is characterized by at­
tributes include the source, destination, and type. The logical entities
include the IoT applications that are modelled as a series of modules
with their attributes, and they have been stimulated by the classes of
AppModule, AppEdge, and AppLoop. The AppModule and the AppEdge
classes are utilized to model the IoT services and the relationship
between them, respectively. Besides, the AppLoop class is used to
determine a set of the IoT services according to the user’s favorite
workflow starting from the beginning of the loop to the IoT service
where the loop finishes. The control entities include two classes of
Controller and ModuleMapping for placing the IoT applications on the fog
nodes. We use the ModuleMapping class to implement the WOA-FSP al­
gorithm to find an efficient placement plan. The Controller class launches
the IoT applications on the fog resources according to the placement
plan and then it gathers the performance metrics such as service delay,
energy consumption, and resource usage during the simulation process.
Also, we performed the simulation experiments on a personal com­
puter with Intel Core i7 2.4 GHz CPU, 1 TB disk, and 8 GB of RAM
running Windows 10-64bit. Besides, we used the random uniform dis­
tribution to generate the synthetic dataset for simulation experiments.
Therefore, we set the properties of resource demands for IoT services
and fog resource capabilities, according to Tables 4 and 5, respectively.
5.2.

One of the proposed cost-efficient IoT service placement algorithm
applications is robotic assistance, which is an essential aspect of Industry
4.0. For example, various surveillance equipment, including IP and
analogue cameras, are installed in smart factories. Industrial robots
analyze the taken photos by these cameras and then extract features for
taking appropriate emergency decisions (M. Afrin, Jin, Rahman, Tian, &
Kulkarni, 2019). On the one hand, image quality can be affected by
weather, lighting condition, or being in an outdoor or an indoor posi­
tion. On the other hand, the utilized equipment for capturing the image
could be in a different technology or brand. These conditions lead to
images with different qualities that may suffer from loss of information.
As a result, many image processing techniques and their services should
be considered to enhance the quality of the images and recover the lost
information. Image Enhancement methods for colour image enhance­
ment include Homomorphic Filtering, Contrast Stretching, Retinex,
Wavelet Multiscale Transform, and Histogram Equalization (Vishwa­
karma & Mishra, 2012). Fog nodes are responsible for processing the
received images from the robots. Then the proposed service placement
algorithm monitors the requirements of the requested services and the
capabilities of available fog nodes to determine an efficient service
placement strategy. Finally, the improved and recovered images are sent
back to the robots for further analysis and emergency decision making.

(SA) to solve the IoT service placement problem.
• BA-FSP (Lin et al., 2020): This strategy models the food-searching
behaviour of bats for deploying weighted fog devices to achieve a
better solution in polynomial time.

6. Conclusion
In this study, we addressed the service placement problem using an
autonomic methodology for deploying IoT applications on the virtual­
